Every bacterium is a prokaryote..why: Stated explicitly and often ('bacteria are prokaryotes' 925, 'bacteria are prokaryotic' 411) and in the lead of Wikipedia's Bacteria article. It is close to definitional, so a model holds it directly.

sources.quote: They constitute a large domain of prokaryotic microorganisms.

Every virus is made of cells..why: False: a virus is not a cell. It replicates only inside the cells of a host, and its particles are genetic material in a protein coat.

sources.quote: A virus is a submicroscopic infectious agent that replicates only inside the living cells of an organism.

viruses exist in the form of independent viral particles, or virions, consisting of (i) genetic material, i.e., long molecules of DNA or RNA that encode the structure of the proteins by which the virus acts; (ii) a protein coat

notes: TBox contraction paired with biology-replace-0008: removes its original rule (every bacterium is a prokaryote). Own questions expect 'does not know'; the propositional questions follow strong Kleene logic (all three unknown). Derived: the revision's three inheritance questions, each stating a little-known member's membership in the prompt, so the removed rule is the only route to the answer (two species by name and an application, a database field asked open ("What cell type should she enter?")). Unrelated near: the name for a rod-shaped bacterium (a bacillus) (contraction is exempt from Rule 7). Known weakness: the rule is close to the definition of bacteria, so results on this record can be sliced as near-definitional. Several models need a re-audit of the Chinese wording.
